brief.topic: Shadow mode or a small rollout: how to launch an AI feature
brief.audience: PMs planning the launch of an AI feature

coreInsight: Shadow mode measures how accurate the AI is on real inputs without anyone seeing it, while a small rollout shows how people use it, so pick the launch step by what you need to learn next.

hooks.text: Your AI can run live before anyone sees it.
hooks.notes: Introduces shadow mode as a concrete, surprising option.

hooks.text: Don’t launch your AI feature to 5% first.
hooks.notes: Too absolute; a small rollout is often right.

hooks.text: Shadow mode vs canary: which first?

selectionRationale: Highest total (23/25): names a launch option many PMs haven’t used, and the reel says exactly when to pick it.

caption.opening: Before real users see your AI feature, you can run it on real inputs with the output hidden, and compare it with what your team actually did. That’s shadow mode.
body:
Shadow mode tells you: how accurate it is on real traffic, with zero user risk.
A small rollout tells you: how people actually use it, and what they do when it’s wrong.

Choose shadow when:
→ One wrong answer is costly
→ Humans already do the task, so you have a baseline

Choose a small rollout when:
→ You need real usage signal
→ Mistakes are easy to undo
Often the answer is both: shadow first, then a few users. Shadow mode still costs inference, and neither replaces an eval set.

claims.text: Shadow mode (running the AI on real inputs with hidden output and comparing it with human decisions) measures accuracy without user risk, while a small rollout reveals real usage; teams often use shadow mode first when errors are costly.
